MUQATIL:4:17-18/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:4:17-18/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:4:17-18/r2.claim: The sinful deeds here mean associating partners with God; repentance at the moment of death is not accepted, nor is it accepted from those who die disbelieving.

FARRA:v1p257/r11.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p257/r11.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p257/r11.claim: الذين is genitive; a disbeliever's repentance is accepted during illness before death arrives, but not once death has arrived.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p150#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p150#2/r1.speaker: ابن عمر
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p150#2/r1.claim: Ibn Umar says repentance remains available until the death rattle; the verse's arrival of death means the soul has reached the throat.

TAB-FULL:v6p515#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p515#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v6p515#2/r1.claim: Those who repent before death’s throes are accepted; someone who waits until death overwhelms understanding and says “I repent now” does so without genuine repentance, like a deceiver.

TAB-FULL:v6p516/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r1.claim: The verse denies repentance to persistent sinners who wait until death is present, see the angels coming for their souls, and speak while death’s throes have overcome them; this is not a genuine state of repentance.

TAB-FULL:v6p516/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r2.claim: Ibn Umar says repentance remains open until the soul is being driven out; he asks whether the verse’s “arrival” means that driving.

TAB-FULL:v6p516/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says repentance is not accepted once death has become clear to the person.

TAB-FULL:v6p516/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says that the person who says “I repent now” when death arrives has no repentance with God.

TAB-FULL:v6p516/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r5.claim: Abd Allah ibn Amr says repentance is accepted even shortly before death, down to an hour or a moment, and says he heard this from the Prophet.

TAB-FULL:v6p516/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r6.speaker: إبراهيم
TAB-FULL:v6p516/r6.claim: Ibrahim transmits the saying that repentance remains open until the dying person is seized by the throat.

TAB-FULL:v6p518/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r1.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r1.claim: Al-Rabi says the passage’s first clause concerns believers, its middle clause about sinners at death concerns hypocrites, and its final clause concerns unbelievers.

TAB-FULL:v6p518/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r2.speaker: سفيان
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r2.claim: Sufyan says the clause about those who delay repentance until death concerns Muslims, as the verse separately names those who die unbelievers.

TAB-FULL:v6p518/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse first addressed believers but was superseded by 4:48, which bars forgiveness for those dying as unbelievers while leaving monotheists to God’s will.

TAB-FULL:v6p518/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v6p518/r4.claim: Al-Tabari prefers Sufyan’s view that the first clause concerns Muslims: hypocrites are unbelievers, so identifying them here would make the separate clause about dying unbelievers redundant; the wording distinguishes sinners from those called unbelievers.

TAB-FULL:v6p520/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p520/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v6p520/r1.claim: The phrase “those who die unbelievers” is coordinated in the genitive with “those who commit sins”; they are farther from repentance because they remain in unbelief, and God has prepared painful punishment for them.

TAB-FULL:v6p520/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p520/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v6p520/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas explains that people who die as unbelievers are farther from repentance.

TAB-FULL:v6p520/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v6p520/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v6p520/r3.claim: Basran grammarians derive أعتدنا from العتاد, meaning “prepared”; Kufan grammarians say أعتدنا and أعددنا are synonymous, while أليما means painful.

ZAJJAJ:v2p29/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v2p29/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v2p29/r1.claim: Repentance at the moment of death is not accepted because the person can no longer cease the actions needed to make repentance real.

ZAJJAJ:v2p29/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v2p29/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v2p29/r2.claim: Alīman means painful, reaching the utmost degree of pain.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r1.claim: Ibn Amr reports from the Prophet that repentance is accepted as late as an hour or a brief moment before death, despite the verse's warning about death's arrival.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r2.speaker: أبو العالية
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r2.claim: Abu al-Aliya says the warning about those who commit sins applies to hypocrites.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r3.speaker: سفيان الثوري
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r3.claim: Sufyan al-Thawri says the sins in this verse refer to associationism.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r4.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r4.claim: Ibn Umar says repentance remains open until the death rattle begins, which he understands as the moment death arrives.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r5.speaker: سفيان الثوري
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r5.claim: Sufyan glosses the arrival of death as the moment a person sees it.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r6.speaker: عبد الله
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r6.claim: Abdullah says a repentance spoken only once death has arrived will not be accepted.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v3p900/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says 4:48 later barred forgiveness for anyone who dies an unbeliever.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r1.speaker: أبو العالية
IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r1.claim: Abu al-Aliya says those who die as unbelievers are polytheists; similar explanations are reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Rabi ibn Anas.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r3.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r3.claim: Ikrima says anything that causes pain is painful punishment.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r4.speaker: أبو العالية
IBNABIHATIM:v3p901/r4.claim: Abu al-Aliya says alim means painful throughout the Quran; several early authorities are reported to agree.

NAHHAS:v1p442/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p442/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p442/r2.claim: The majority take السيئات as lesser sins; other readings concern those nearing death or sinners generally, with unbelievers singled out.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r10.claim: The passage equates dying unrepentant with repenting only when death arrives, a state recognizable to those present even if the dying person cannot report it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r8.speaker: الجمهور
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r8.claim: Most interpreters say the warning about those who die without repentance was revealed concerning sinful Muslims; al-Rabi says it concerns hypocrites.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r9.speaker: الربيع
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p464/r9.claim: Al-Rabi says this verse was revealed concerning hypocrites.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r1.speaker: الوعيدية
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r1.claim: The Waʿidiyya use this verse to argue that sinful Muslims who postpone repentance until death join disbelievers in afterlife punishment, citing the final clause.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas in Ataa's report interprets the sinful acts here as shirk; Ikrimah likewise transmits from him that the people are polytheists.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r3.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r3.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas says the one saying 'I repent now' is a hypocrite, as the verse then mentions disbelievers.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r4.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr assigns 4:17 to believers, 4:18 to hypocrites, and the clause about dying as disbelievers to unbelievers.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r5.claim: Because the Companion and Successor authorities who witnessed revelation apply the verse to disbelievers or hypocrites, the author rejects extending it to Muslims who pray.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says 4:48 later clarified that those dying in unbelief are denied forgiveness while monotheists remain subject to God's will and hope of pardon.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p390/r7.claim: The author denies that this is abrogation: abrogation is not attributed to Ibn Abbas here; 4:48 specifies that the first verse's apparent generality excludes monotheists.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r1.claim: The phrase 'nor those who die as disbelievers' is genitive by coordination with the earlier noun; it denies them repentance in the afterlife.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r2.claim: After death, repentance is not accepted because responsibility ends and the promised afterlife reward and punishment are seen; this also explains rejection at death.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r3.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the dying person repents at a time when he can no longer act to fulfill repentance.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r4.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r4.claim: Al-Layth explains aʿtadnā as prepared and readied; related forms describe what is present or reserved, a stored grooming case, equipment, and a horse made ready to ride.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r5.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r5.claim: Al-Azhari presents two derivations: a root ʿ-t-d with a separate form, or doubled dāl as in aʿdadtu; he calls an independent ʿatad alongside doubled ʿadad the soundest account.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r6.speaker: امرؤ القيس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v6p392/r6.claim: Imru al-Qays's wording 'I readied for war' with doubled dāl is cited as evidence for the aʿdadt derivation.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:17-19/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:17-19/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:17-19/r4.claim: The denied repentance is for polytheists and hypocrites who persist in sins, or those who die as unbelievers; repentance is not accepted in the afterlife.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:17-19/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:17-19/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:17-19/r5.claim: The following phrase means God has prepared their punishment.

JISHUMI:v2p1493/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r10.claim: One occasion account assigns the opening verses to believers, the middle to hypocrites, and the final verse to disbelievers who die persisting in disbelief.

JISHUMI:v2p1493/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r7.claim: Jahāla is rooted in ignorance, understood as believing a thing to be other than it is; repentance is return, regret over the past, and resolve not to repeat it.

JISHUMI:v2p1493/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r8.claim: Aʿtadnā means prepared; it may derive from a tāʾ substituted for dāl or from ʿatād, equipment set ready for a task.

JISHUMI:v2p1493/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1493/r9.claim: In ولا الذين يموتون, الذين is genitive by coordination with الذين يعملون السوء, with the implied sense: nor those who die.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r1.claim: Repentance is not accepted when a sinner reaches the death throes and says, 'I repent now'; neither is it accepted from those who die as disbelievers.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r2.claim: The author cites the people whose faith did not help once they saw God's punishment, and Pharaoh's failed belief as drowning overtook him.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p185#2/r3.claim: A'tadna means prepared or made ready.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25#2/r1.claim: If 'those' refers only to dying unbelievers, their punishment is eternal; if it includes sinners who delay repentance until death, their punishment is not eternal.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25#2/r2.claim: Aʿtadnā means prepared and made present; the verse's wording indicates that Hell already exists.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r10.speaker: ابن عباس، ابن زيد وجماعة المفسرين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r10.claim: They say the excluded person is one whose death has arrived and who has entered despair, like Pharaoh during drowning.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r11.speaker: الربيع
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r11.claim: Al-Rabi says the first verse addresses believers and the second originally addressed Muslims, then was abrogated by Qur'an 4:48 and 4:116, which denies forgiveness for associating partners and leaves other believers to God's will.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r12.claim: The abrogation claim is weak: although phrased as a report, the verse establishes a legal ruling, and no abrogation is needed because it excludes only repentance at death, not forgiveness for an unrepentant sinner under Qur'an 4:48 and 4:116.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r13.speaker: أبو المعالي وآخرون
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r13.claim: A repentant person who turns back before death has the status of the repentant; al-Maali says the scriptural promise makes salvation likely, while others say forgiveness is certain.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p25/r14.claim: One who waits until death is not treated as repentant: an unbeliever remains eternally in punishment, while a sinful believer is under God's will, with fear of punishment prevailing though some are certainly forgiven by grace.

TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r2.claim: Accepted repentance does not extend to persistent sinners who delay until death's signs and hope of life have ended; at that point they say they repent now.

TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r3.claim: Exegetes agree the verse concerns sinful Muslims, apart from a report from al-Rabīʿ that it concerns hypocrites; the author rejects that because hypocrites are unbelievers, separately named in the next clause.

TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r4.claim: The unbelievers named afterward are those who die in unbelief and regret only after death; God has prepared for them painful punishment.

TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r5.claim: Repentance at death is invalid because the dying person is compelled to choose good and abandon evil, outside moral responsibility and thus outside the conditions of repentance; the afterlife is similarly beyond obligation.

TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r6.claim: The wording “prepared a painful punishment” does not prove that sinful believers who die unrepentant must be punished: it can mean they merit Hell, may refer to the nearer unbelievers, or describe what justice would impose absent divine pardon.

TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18#3/r7.claim: The promise to forgive lesser sins whoever God wills applies only to monotheist believers who die with an unrepented major sin; the righteous, repentant, and unbelievers are not in that class.

TABRISI:4:17-18#4/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#4/r1.speaker: الربيع
TABRISI:4:17-18#4/r1.claim: Al-Rabīʿ claims this verse was abrogated by the promise that God forgives lesser sins for whom He wills in 4:48 and 4:116.

TABRISI:4:17-18#4/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18#4/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18#4/r2.claim: The author rejects abrogation because this verse states a report about what God has prepared, and reports cannot be abrogated as legal commands can.

TABRISI:4:17-18/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18/r2.claim: Aʿtadnā may derive from aʿdadnā with tāʾ substituting for dāl, or may be a verb formed from ʿatād, equipment; the latter is illustrated by ʿAdī b. al-Riqāʿ's poetry.

TABRISI:4:17-18/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:4:17-18/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:4:17-18/r3.claim: The phrase about those who die is grammatically genitive by coordination with the earlier phrase, with an implied repetition of “nor for.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r1.claim: Sayi'at in this verse means associating partners with God.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r2.speaker: أبو العالية وسعيد بن جبير
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r2.claim: Another interpretation takes sayi'at as hypocrisy.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r3.speaker: سفيان الثوري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r3.claim: Sayi'at may mean Muslims' sins; he cites the following phrase about those who die as unbelievers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r4.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r4.claim: “When death comes” means the onset of death's agony.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r5.speaker: أبو سليمان الدمشقي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r5.claim: Another interpretation is when a person sees the angels taking the soul.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r6.speaker: علي بن أبي طلحة عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v2p38/r6.claim: God later revealed 4:116: pardon is barred for those who die as polytheists, while monotheists remain subject to God's will; on that reading this verse is abrogated for believers.

RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r1.claim: Repentance is not accepted once death's signs and terrors arrive, as shown also by the rejected belief of Pharaoh at drowning and by the deathbed pleas in other passages.

RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r2.speaker: أبو أيوب
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r2.claim: Abu Ayyub transmits from the Prophet that God accepts a servant's repentance until the soul reaches the throat and rattles there.

RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r3.speaker: عطاء
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r3.claim: Ata says repentance is accepted even until a moment before death, as short as the time it takes a camel to be milked.

RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r4.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r4.claim: Hasan relates that Satan vowed to mislead Adam's children while their souls remained in their bodies, and God vowed to keep repentance open until the soul rattles in the throat.

RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p6#2/r5.claim: When death comes means when its signs and approach are present, as in the command about an inheritance when death comes in 2:180.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r1.claim: Razi challenges the Mu'tazilite claim that resurrection makes knowledge of God necessary: observing revival and fire does not prove God caused them, since those conclusions remain inferential.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r2.claim: Even if resurrection knowledge were necessary, the Mu'tazilites have not shown why that ends duty: a servant might still sin while believing God is merciful and unaffected by human obedience.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r3.claim: Their distinction between theoretical and necessary knowledge is weak: if the possibility of the opposite remains, there is only opinion; if it does not, theoretical knowledge cannot be weaker than necessary knowledge.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r4.claim: God acts as He wills: by grace He promised acceptance at some times and by justice announced rejection at another, and He can reverse either judgment, as 21:23 says.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7#2/r5.claim: A three-part division follows: repentance from ignorant sin is promised acceptance in 4:17; repentance only at death is rejected; deliberate sinners who repent earlier are left to God's will, as in 4:48.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r1.speaker: المحققون
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r1.claim: The investigators say nearness to death and its pain do not itself bar repentance; the true barrier is witnessing events that make knowledge of God unavoidable and remove moral responsibility.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r2.claim: People revived after death, including Israelites and Job's children, were again charged with duties, so experiencing death does not itself end accountability.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r3.claim: Death's pains resemble colic or labor, which do not end responsibility; rising distress should make repentance more likely to be accepted, since God responds to the distressed in 27:62.

RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p7/r4.claim: At death, witnessed terrors make knowledge of God necessary and end obligation; people of the afterlife likewise cannot repent even before entering Hell because their knowledge is necessary.

RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r1.claim: The phrase about those who die as disbelievers can mean people near death, whose faith too is rejected, or unbelievers who die in disbelief and cannot repent in the afterlife.

RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r2.speaker: الوعيدية
RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r2.claim: Threat proponents argue that the conjunction separates sinners who repent at death from disbelievers, yet the same painful threat covers both; they also say forgiveness without repentance would make the warning pointless.

RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p8/r3.claim: Razi answers that the nearest referent of the prepared painful punishment can be disbelievers alone; because their unbelief is worse, they may receive added humiliation beyond sinful believers.

RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r1.claim: The absence of repentance at death still leaves punishment or forgiveness possible and thus warns the sinner, like 4:48; moreover, the Mu'tazilites themselves reject arguments from what a text merely implies.

RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r2.claim: Because disbelievers are conjoined separately from those who sin, the verse refutes the Kharijite claim that a Muslim sinner is an unbeliever; the hypocrite reading also fails because hypocrites are unbelievers, as 63:1 says.

RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r3.speaker: أصحابنا
RAZI-FULL:v10p9/r3.claim: Aʿtadna means prepared or made ready; the past tense in 4:18 and the parallel descriptions of Hell in 2:24 and 3:131 are used to argue that Hell is already created.

QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r10.claim: An alternative reads ‘sins’ as disbelief, making the verse deny acceptance both to disbelievers repenting at death and to those repenting after death on Judgment Day.

QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r12.claim: Here, those committing sins are people who persist until the death struggle and seeing the Angel of Death; repentance then is too late.

QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r13.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r13.claim: The phrase describing painful punishment means painful and lasting; the surrounding discussion has already been explained.

QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r8.speaker: ابن عباس وابن زيد وجمهور المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r8.claim: Repentance is not accepted once death appears and hope is gone, as Pharaoh’s confession while drowning did not benefit him; obligation has ended.

QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:4:17-18#3/r9.claim: Those who die in disbelief have no repentance in the afterlife and face eternal punishment; sinful believers face punishment without eternity if the sins mean lesser sins.

BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r1.claim: Last-minute repentance by sinners and death in disbelief are treated alike to stress that repentance at that point is not accepted.

BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r2.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r2.claim: Another interpretation identifies the first group as sinful believers, the next as hypocrites whose disbelief and misconduct are compounded, and the final group as disbelievers.

BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:4:18/r3.claim: The verse confirms their repentance is not accepted and says their painful punishment has been prepared; i'tadad means preparation from 'atad, equipment, and may derive from a form of a'adda.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r1.claim: Repentance is not accepted once the dying person sees the causes of death and the angel of death: responsibility has ended, and the act is compelled rather than chosen.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r2.claim: Acceptance is reward and promise, and can only apply to a voluntary act.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r3.claim: The phrase about those who die disbelieving coordinates grammatically with the earlier relative clause: there is no repentance for either group.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r4.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr assigns the first verse to believers, the middle one to hypocrites, and the last to unbelievers.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p212/r5.claim: Some codices write the phrase with two lām letters; the following demonstrative is a subject whose predicate is that painful punishment has been prepared.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p563/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p563/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p563/r6.claim: The verse denies acceptance to the sinner who delays repentance until despair at death, and to the person who dies in disbelief; Pharaoh is an example of the first.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r1.claim: He equates the deathbed with the afterlife because both lie beyond the point of choice and religious responsibility.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r2.speaker: المعتزلة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r2.claim: They say knowledge of God becomes necessary through witnessing afterlife terrors, removing the basis for religious obligation and choice.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r3.claim: The author says approaching death does not itself end responsibility: Israelites were resurrected and held accountable after death, and death’s pain is no greater than other severe pain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r4.claim: Near-death distress could even help a person repent; God may accept at some times and withhold acceptance at others by sovereign choice.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r5.speaker: الربيع
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r5.claim: He says the verse originally concerned Muslims and was superseded by the statement that God may forgive lesser sins, leaving believers’ fate to divine will.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r6.claim: The author says no abrogation need be claimed: 4:18 does not say that no sinner without accepted repentance can be forgiven; he also notes that reports are not normally abrogated.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p564/r7.claim: The two coordinated groups are distinct: ‘nor’ negates the rule separately for each group, and the phrase ‘while they are unbelievers’ belongs to those who die in that state.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī gives two readings of those doing sins: disbelievers, because the next clause says they die as unbelievers, or Muslim grave sinners, with unbelief used as severe threat language.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r2.claim: The author calls al-Zamakhsharī’s options contradictory: his earlier explanation requires two groups, but this discussion collapses them into one or treats unbelief figuratively.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r3.claim: He says the strained interpretation serves Muʿtazilite doctrine by guaranteeing punishment for grave sinners and violates syntax and the apparent sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r4.claim: The present tense ‘they do’ signals persistence in sins until death; ‘I repent now’ is repentance only upon seeing death and is therefore defensive, not accepted.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r5.claim: Another reading makes ‘I repent now’ conditional rather than decisive, which is why it is not accepted.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p565/r6.claim: ‘Repentance is not for them’ means their repentance is not accepted, not that they cannot repent; the second group literally dies in disbelief and cannot repent afterward in this world.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r1.claim: ‘They die’ may mean they approach death, just as ‘death came’ can refer to its signs; then unbelief, like repentance, is not accepted at that point.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r2.claim: ‘Those’ may refer to both groups, who share a prepared punishment though one punishment ends and the other lasts forever, or only to the nearest-mentioned unbelievers.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r3.claim: The first reading warns the sinner who delays repentance until death by pairing him with an unbeliever; the second ties the threat to dying in disbelief.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r4.claim: The apparent mention of punishment already prepared indicates that Hell is created, a topic the author says he discussed earlier.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r5.claim: He says the parallel wording of a prepared threat and God’s promise to accept repentance shows both outcomes will certainly occur.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r6.claim: The author says this subtly imports the Muʿtazilite claim that grave sinners without repentance must certainly be punished; the nearest antecedent may instead be unbelievers.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p566/r7.claim: Even if the threat includes unrepentant Muslim sinners, it does not require punishment: God may punish or forgive them under the decisive verse about lesser sins.

SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r1.claim: الذين is genitive and coordinated with الذين يعملون: repentance is unavailable to late penitents at death and to those dying disbelievers; the first group means hypocrites.

SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r2.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ makes الذين nominative as a subject and أولئك and what follows its predicate, treating the preceding lām as emphatic.

SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r3.claim: That parse fails against the written form: an emphatic lām before the article would be للذين, but the text has ولا الذين with the negative particle.

SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:4:18#2/r4.claim: أولئك is a subject and أعتدنا its predicate; it may refer to the nearest group alone or both groups, and أعتدنا means ‘prepared.’

SAMIN-DURR:4:18/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:4:18/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:4:18/r1.claim: حتى begins a new conditional clause setting the endpoint for persistent sin: when death comes, they say they repent; it does not govern إذا as a preposition.

SAMIN-DURR:4:18/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:4:18/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:4:18/r2.claim: A prepositional حتى fails because it would govern a conditional clause, which cannot be governed from before; Ibn Mālik’s examples at 39:71 and 10:22 are discussed, as is 4:6.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r1.claim: A disbeliever who dies in disbelief gains nothing from remorse or repentance and cannot ransom himself even with earth’s weight in gold.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r2.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو العالية والربيع بن أنس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliya, and al-Rabi ibn Anas say the verse concerns people who die in polytheism.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r3.speaker: أبو ذر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p238/r3.claim: The Prophet says repentance or forgiveness remains possible until the barrier falls, meaning the soul leaves while the person is associating partners with God.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r12.claim: Repentance is not accepted from persistent sinners who do not return soon and wait until death reaches the throat; foregrounding the person facing death creates suspense and fear.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r13.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r13.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r13.claim: A dying sinner's claim to repent now may be spoken aloud, as Pharaoh did, or held in the heart; the verse sharply urges haste.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r14.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r14.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r14.claim: The same ruling covers those who die as unbelievers, literally or figuratively, without repenting, including at the death-rattle.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r15.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r15.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p227/r15.claim: The verse groups persistent sin and unbelief to deter sinning, because withdrawal from sin becomes difficult after committing it; both face painful punishment, while unrepentant believers remain subject to God's will.

DURR-FULL:v2p460/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r1.claim: In the account of the repentant killer, after killing one hundred he seeks repentance, leaves his corrupt town, dies en route to a good town, and is assigned to the nearer community after God moves the towns closer or farther.

DURR-FULL:v2p460/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r2.claim: The Prophet says God accepts a servant's repentance until the soul reaches the throat.

DURR-FULL:v2p460/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r3.speaker: رجل من الصحابة
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r3.claim: A Companion heard that repentance is accepted if made before the soul reaches the throat.

DURR-FULL:v2p460/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r4.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r4.claim: Repentance remains open until death begins; Ibn Umar reads the verse and explains that the moment of death means the onset of dying.

DURR-FULL:v2p460/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r5.claim: Repentance is not accepted once death is present.

DURR-FULL:v2p460/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p460/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the people in the first clause as polytheists; another transmitted wording says they have no repentance at death and disbelievers are farther from it.

DURR-FULL:v2p461/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r1.claim: The later verse 4:48 reserves those who die as unbelievers from forgiveness but leaves monotheists to God's will, so they need not despair.

DURR-FULL:v2p461/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r2.speaker: ابن عمرو
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r2.claim: Any sin between heaven and earth is forgiven if the servant repents before death.

DURR-FULL:v2p461/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r3.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r3.claim: A saying holds that repentance remains open until a person is choked by death.

DURR-FULL:v2p461/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r4.speaker: ابن عمرو
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r4.claim: One who repents before death by a breath's span is forgiven; when challenged with this verse, Ibn Amr says he is conveying what he heard from the Prophet.

DURR-FULL:v2p461/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r5.speaker: أبو ذر
DURR-FULL:v2p461/r5.claim: God accepts repentance until the veil falls, which the Prophet explains as the soul leaving while its owner is a polytheist.

BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r1.claim: The Persian verse calls the present world a prison for souls and urges travel toward the soul's open country.

BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r2.speaker: العطار
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r2.claim: ʿAṭṭār urges removing the veil from the sun, crossing bodily Mount Qāf toward the spiritual kingdom, and refusing pride in this false realm where wealth and honor pass.

BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r3.claim: Repentance is unavailable to those who continue sinning until death throes and see the angel of death; that is compulsion rather than choice.

BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r4.claim: The denial also applies to those who die unbelievers and repent only near death or on seeing punishment; both groups face prepared, painful punishment.

BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r5.claim: Equating a deathbed procrastinator with an unbeliever stresses that neither has valid repentance then, urging sinners to seek forgiveness promptly.

BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r6.speaker: جلال الدين رومي
BURSEVI:v2p143#2/r6.claim: Rūmī says to repent for earlier sins and trust that God accepts; divine care makes a person hasten to repent when even a small reminder moves him.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r1.claim: Repentance is not accepted from people persisting in sins when death arrives and they see the irreversibility of return and the Angel of Death; saying 'I repent now' is not treated as genuine repentance.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r10.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r10.claim: Some distinguish repentance from faith: repentance renews an existing covenant with God and may be accepted at despair, while faith initiates a new covenant; the Bazzaziyya calls acceptance of repentance, unlike faith, the sound position.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r11.speaker: القاضي عبدالصمد الحنفي
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r11.claim: Al-Qadi ʿAbd al-Samad al-Hanafi says Sufis hold that faith still benefits at the sight of punishment; Ibn al-ʿArabi likewise validates faith under compulsion, and Ibn ʿUmar hoped well for a polytheist who gurgled Islam.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r2.claim: The plural 'sins' reflects repeated occurrence over an extended time rather than all categories of sin; the previously mentioned evil is one type of sin.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r3.claim: The verse says 'he said' rather than 'he repented' to avoid counting this last-moment utterance as repentance; the conditional clause after حتى marks the limit of the preceding denial.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r4.claim: The dying state resembles the afterlife, which begins with death: this world is a place of action without requital, while the next is requital without action.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r5.claim: The second group is also denied acceptance; mentioning them alongside last-moment repenters warns that delayed repentance is nearly worthless, and repeating the negative may suggest its futility is even more emphatic.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r6.speaker: أكثر أهل العلم
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r6.claim: Most scholars understand the first group to include sinful believers and disbelievers, and the second group to mean disbelievers only.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r7.claim: Other interpretations take both groups as disbelievers, both as sinners with 'disbelievers' used for severity, or both as including the two groups with the label based on predominance.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r8.speaker: الربيع
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r8.claim: Al-Rabiʿ and Abu al-Aliya report that the preceding repentance verse concerned believers, this verse's first group hypocrites, and its final group polytheists; the author calls this weak because persistent hypocrites cannot repent, while repentant ones are no different from others.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p239#2/r9.claim: The verse is evidence that repentance at the point of despair is not accepted, but scholars dispute whether such repentance remains valid while hope, regret, and resolve to stop are possible.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r1.speaker: أبو ذر
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r1.claim: A report from Abu Dharr says God accepts repentance or forgives a servant until the veil falls; the Prophet explains that the veil falls when the soul departs while the person is still an idolater, supporting repentance before that point.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r2.claim: The verse appears to support rejection of last-moment repentance; some answer that it denies guaranteed acceptance rather than guaranteeing rejection, leaving the matter under God's will, while 4:48 excludes the persistent disbeliever from forgiveness.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r3.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r3.claim: Some say the dying sinner only says 'I repent now' without true repentance; even if قال has another rhetorical purpose, the word 'now' may show that resolve not to return, a condition of valid repentance, is absent.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r4.claim: The referent of 'those' in the punishment clause is parsed as the two groups mentioned, and the preparation of painful punishment is rendered with emphasis on its being readied for them.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r5.speaker: قيل
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r5.claim: A lexical explanation says أعتدنا means أعددنا, with the dāl changed to tāʾ; the adjective painful intensifies the punishment, and the indefinite noun magnifies it.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r6.speaker: المعتزلة
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r6.claim: The Muʿtazilites use the verse to argue that believers who die with major sins unrepented must be punished; the response is that preparing Hell does not state that God will certainly admit them, and may mean punishment if He does not pardon them.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r7.speaker: الربيع
ALUSI-FULL:v4p240/r7.claim: Al-Rabiʿ says the verse was abrogated by 4:48, which says God forgives what is below associating partners to whom He wills.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p241/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p241/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p241/r1.claim: The abrogation claim is rejected because أعتدنا is a report, and reports are not abrogated.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p241/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p241/r2.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v4p241/r2.claim: An alternative reading makes 'those' refer only to those who die as disbelievers, or to both groups understood as hypocrites first and polytheists second.

ELMALILI:4:17-18/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r2.claim: Repentance is not promised for those who repeatedly commit wrong and wait until death arrives before saying they repent, nor for those who die as disbelievers.

ELMALILI:4:17-18/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r3.claim: For deliberate sinners who do not repent soon and make sin habitual, but repent before the death throes and despair of life, acceptance is possible by God's will but is not certain.

ELMALILI:4:17-18/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r4.claim: Faith adopted before the death throes, while a person still hopes to live, is accepted; faith adopted in despair during the death throes is not.

ELMALILI:4:17-18/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r5.claim: A new believer needs time after faith to acquire good deeds.

ELMALILI:4:17-18/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:4:17-18/r6.claim: A sinful believer's repentance at the last breath may be accepted, as in the call not to despair of God's mercy (39:53), but acceptance is still not guaranteed.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p278/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p278/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p278/r2.claim: Some held the two qualifiers abrogated by 4:48; most treat ignorance as a descriptive feature of wrongdoing by believers. A report from Qatāda says the Companions regarded every disobedience, deliberate or not, as ignorance; Ibn ʿĀshūr says both qualifiers advise normal conduct rather than condition acceptance, and the two verses leave no middle category.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p280/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p280/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p280/r2.claim: The following statement denies acceptance for repentance made at death, when life is despaired of, because repentance should lead to righteous conduct in this world and has no benefit once life is lost.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r1.claim: Faith is repentance from unbelief and its noblest form; an unbeliever who dies in unbelief is not accepted in repentance from it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r2.speaker: العلماء
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r2.claim: One interpretation takes the verse literally: death alone prevents an unbeliever from converting; the denied repentance is remorse on Judgment Day, while faith before death is accepted.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r3.claim: A report in the Sahih recounts that the Prophet urged Abu Talib to profess God's oneness at death, but Abu Jahl and Ibn Abi Umayya urged him to remain on Abdul Muttalib's religion; his final words affirmed it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r4.claim: The contrast between the two clauses distinguishes a person who reaches death from one who actually dies an unbeliever.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r5.claim: A living convert's inward faith and spoken profession bring him into the Muslim community, strengthening it and making Islam known among unbelievers.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r6.speaker: العلماء
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r6.claim: A second interpretation equates the unbeliever and sinful believer: neither can repent once death approaches; syntax requires reading 'die' as approach death, like other Qur'anic usage.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r7.speaker: العلماء
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r7.claim: Advocates of the second interpretation cite Pharaoh's profession of faith while drowning as an instance of faith not being accepted at that moment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p281/r8.claim: Pharaoh's case shows that faith after punishment descends is useless; Jonah's people are the exception, and drowning was punishment for Pharaoh and his army.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r1.claim: God is not compelled to accept repentance: as sovereign, He may accept what He promised or refuse repentance in cases He states will not be forgiven.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r2.speaker: بعضهم
TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r2.claim: One commentator argues that Pharaoh's final repentance is not explicitly rejected and that God's broad mercy makes eternal rejection implausible.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#10/r3.claim: The argument fails because 4:18 excludes repentance at death; such last-moment regret is insincere, prompted by seeing punishment arrive.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r1.claim: Judgment-day regret and requests to return do not prove accepted repentance: the Qur'an says the sinners would return to their old conduct and are lying.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r2.claim: Repentance corresponds to social moral reform: external causes enable change, the person leaves the bad state, and the corrupt disposition is replaced by virtue.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#11/r3.claim: Repentance changes the soul and prepares it for happiness by removing inward evils; it does not by itself cancel religious laws or rulings.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r1.claim: Some legal consequences are lifted when legislation itself ties them to repentance, as with offenders who repent and those who repent before capture for violent corruption.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r2.claim: Repentance helps escape sin's ruin and attain success, while preserving hope; people need hope and fear in balance, and repentance revives one weakened by despair.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#12/r3.claim: Repentance does not encourage planned sin: someone intending to sin and repent all along has never truly renounced the sin or regretted it, but has made one deceitful act.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r1.claim: Real repentance requires knowing the sin is harmful, regretting it, and following with good acts that oppose it and demonstrate a genuine turn.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r2.claim: Repentance is a voluntary return possible only in worldly life; it cannot occur after choice ends, and human claims require the rights-holder's consent.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#13/r3.claim: God cannot erase another person's property, honor, or life-right without their consent; conversion to Islam, however, erases prior sins and branch-level consequences.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r1.claim: Those who establish harmful practices or mislead others cannot fully undo their sin, because its continuing effects remain beyond their power to remove.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r2.claim: Repentance can wipe out sins and, with faith and good deeds, even turn them into good deeds, but avoiding sin is better than erasing it later.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r3.claim: Sins ultimately follow satanic whispers; the purified sincere servants have a special station of servitude unlike ordinary righteous penitents.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:4:17-18#14/r4.claim: A report in al-Faqih says God accepts repentance before death by a year, month, day, or hour, and even until the soul reaches the throat.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r1.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r1.claim: Al-Sadiq explains the excluded repentance as one made when a person has witnessed the afterlife's reality; al-Tabataba'i says awareness of it is decisive, while the unaware may still repent.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r2.claim: Al-Baqir says that when the soul reaches the throat, a knowledgeable person has no repentance, though an ignorant person still may repent.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r3.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r3.claim: The report from Abu Dharr says God accepts repentance until the barrier falls, which the Prophet explains as the soul leaving while the person is a polytheist.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:4:17-18#15/r4.claim: A report transmitted by al-Hasan says Iblis vowed not to leave Adam while his soul remained, and God vowed not to bar repentance during that time.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r1.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r1.claim: Al-Baqir says no one escapes sins except by acknowledging them, and that regret itself is sufficient repentance.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r2.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r2.claim: Sincere repentance makes God love the servant and conceal the sin: He makes the recording angels forget and commands bodily witnesses and places to hide it.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r3.claim: Al-Baqir says a believer's sins are forgiven, and God repeatedly forgives the believer who genuinely regrets, seeks forgiveness, and returns; he warns against despairing believers.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r4.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r4.claim: Al-Sadiq says acceptance requires fidelity to the covenant; even a knowingly committed sin is done in ignorance because the sinner risks himself, as with Joseph's brothers.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#16/r5.claim: Al-Tabataba'i finds the report text confused; its apparent point is that repentance must restrain a person from sin, even if only for a time, while “in ignorance” explains all sin.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#4/r3.claim: At death, when afterlife signs appear, a new profession of faith has no benefit; the commentary supports this with 6:158 and the people who declared faith only upon seeing punishment.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r3.claim: The second verse omits 'upon God,' hinting that these people have lost special divine mercy; its plural 'sins' also signals that their misdeeds are being counted and retained.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r4.claim: Describing them as continually committing sins until death can indicate that procrastination itself is repeated sin, persistence in the act, or the usual recurrence of similar sins.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r5.claim: The singular wording 'when death comes to one of them' belittles the matter: people act as they please and imagine that uttering 'I repent now' at death makes them safe.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#6/r6.claim: 'Now' indicates that seeing death and the reality of judgment itself prompts the speaker's declaration of repentance, whether or not he consciously remembers it.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r1.claim: Deathbed regret is compelled by despair at worldly life and the terror of what is coming, when worldly choice has ended; it is too late for repentance.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r2.claim: The second excluded case is one who persists in disbelief until death; posthumous faith cannot save such a person, as other verses also state.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r3.claim: The denial of helpers in 3:91 also denies intercession for those who die disbelieving.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r4.claim: The qualifier “while disbelievers” leaves open forgiveness for a sinful believer after death through intercession: human repentance ends at death, but God's merciful return need not.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r5.claim: The two verses principally describe God's acceptance or refusal of repentance toward people, while describing their repentance toward God only secondarily.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r6.claim: The demonstrative distances these people from divine nearness and honor; “prepared” can mean either preparation or a promise of punishment.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r7.claim: The Qur'an gives repentance a developed account of its reality; other religions recognize conversion from disbelief as faith without analyzing it as repentance, while Christian atonement teaching can imply repentance is useless.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#7/r8.claim: The Church later went to the opposite extreme by trading in indulgences and having religious authorities forgive confessed sins.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r1.claim: Human beings are absolutely poor before God and possess no independent power over benefit, harm, life, death, or resurrection.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r2.claim: The Qur'an depicts humanity as lowered into misery and distance, and needing rescue from that condition.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r3.claim: Repentance is return from distance and misery to God: faith turns from shirk, while good action turns from sins; nearness and happiness require both.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r4.claim: Because people are inherently needy, their return requires God's preceding enablement and assistance, described as God first turning to them so they may repent.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r5.claim: After a servant repents, God's second repentance is acceptance through forgiveness and purification from sin and distance.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#8/r6.claim: God's repentance is one act of mercy, described as preceding or following only relative to the servant's turn; it can also occur without a prior servant repentance, as in intercession.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r1.claim: God's will to turn toward people contrasts with the desire of those who follow their passions to lead them far astray.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r2.claim: Because nearness is relative, even impeccable prophets can repent by moving from one spiritual station to a higher one.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r3.claim: Many Qur'anic passages apply God's repentance broadly as forgiving and accepting the turn of servants.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r4.claim: God's mercy removing sins and the servant's return from sins both count as repentance; true preaching therefore calls people to repent from sins as well as shirk.

TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:4:17-18#9/r5.claim: God's repentance is unowed favor; its apparent obligation is only the certainty created by God's own promises, which He does not break.

ASAD-NOTES:4:17#n16/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:4:17#n16/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:4:17#n16/r1.claim: The literal wording describes someone saying this when death approaches.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:4:17/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:4:17/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:4:17/r4.claim: Repentance made only in life's final moments after confronting death and the unseen is rejected because it seeks escape from visible punishment rather than expressing faith and sincere regret, with no time left for further moral testing.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:4:17/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:4:17/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:4:17/r5.claim: Repentance after a lifetime of rejecting true religion, made only after seeing the afterlife, is also rejected because it is not grounded in faith in the unseen or sincere remorse; other verses confirm this rule.

STUDYQURAN:4:17/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r1.claim: The commentary links vv. 17–18 with 6:54 and 16:119; doing evil includes general disbelief and particular disobedience.

STUDYQURAN:4:17/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r15.speaker: Some
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r15.claim: Some hold that vv. 17–18 were abrogated by 4:48 and 4:116, which leave sins other than idolatry open to forgiveness.

STUDYQURAN:4:17/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r16.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r16.claim: Repenting from a major sin does not necessarily avert its prescribed worldly punishment.

STUDYQURAN:4:17/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r6.speaker: Some; others; still others
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r6.claim: Views differ on when repentance is quick enough: during health, before death is certain, or any time before death.

STUDYQURAN:4:17/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r7.claim: A hadith saying repentance remains open until the sun rises in the West supports a broader time frame.

STUDYQURAN:4:17/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r8.speaker: God
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r8.claim: A sacred hadith likewise says God does not bar Adam's repentance while his spirit remains in him.

STUDYQURAN:4:17/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:17/r9.claim: Because true repentance requires amends and resolve not to return, one should repent while mentally lucid, physically able, and morally responsible.

STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r1.claim: The sūrah was revealed in Madinah around the fourth year after the hijrah, following the Battle of Uḥud between Muslims and the still-idolatrous Quraysh of Makkah.

STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r2.claim: Its name reflects its extensive treatment of women’s rights, marriage, marital relations, and inheritance.

STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r4.claim: The sūrah ranks among Islam’s most important and foundational works for jurisprudence.

STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:4:intro/r5.claim: The sūrah discusses hypocrites and Jews who turned against Madinah’s Muslim community after Uhud, when Muslims were defeated by Quraysh.
